conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'll be taking care of you during your stay. You were admitted for frequent diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had about 10 watery bowel movements a day for the past few days. They’re yellow-green but not bloody. No stomach pain, just really weak and short of breath walking up stairs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned this feels similar to your past C. diff episodes. We’ve sent stool tests to check for infections, including C. diff, parasites, and viruses. So far, no fever or vomiting—good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had C. diff five times before. Always just diarrhea, no pain. But this time, I stopped my Lasix because I felt dehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re holding your Lasix for now. Your kidney function is a bit worse—creatinine is 3.1, up from your usual 2.0. We’re giving IV fluids to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my transplant okay? I’m worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your transplant team was consulted. They recommend continuing tacrolimus and sirolimus. We’ll check your levels tomorrow morning to make sure they’re in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. Should I restart my blood pressure pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We’ll wait until your fluid levels stabilize. Your blood pressure is stable now at 103/77.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking all my meds as prescribed. I just stopped the Lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing the right thing. We also checked a chest X-ray—your lungs are clear, so the shortness of breath is likely from weakness and dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not starting antibiotics yet. Your tests so far show no infection, and you’re not running a fever. We’ll treat the symptoms for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your C. diff test came back negative. So did stool cultures for Salmonella, Shigella, and parasites. CMV test was also negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? What else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might be related to your immunosuppressants—sirolimus or tacrolimus. But your tacrolimus level was 5.9, which is within range. Sirolimus was 12.2, also okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what do we do now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep giving IV fluids and start loperamide for the diarrhea. Since you’ve had multiple episodes, we’re scheduling a GI follow-up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. Can I start eating normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please try to eat soft, bland foods. Staying hydrated is key. We’re also monitoring your kidney function closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is improving—down to 2.2. That’s a good sign. Your latest CBC shows your hemoglobin is stable at 9.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that low? I remember being anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have chronic anemia from kidney disease. But it’s stable, so no transfusion needed. We’ll continue your usual meds like citalopram and febuxostat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on aspirin, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, and metoprolol—all continued. Your blood pressure is improving, so we’ll restart amlodipine today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve only had two loose stools today. Is that progress?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. The loperamide is helping. We’ll switch you to oral fluids soon and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to see one more set of labs tomorrow. Your kidney function is nearly back to baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news. Your creatinine is now 1.5—back to your normal range. Your diarrhea has slowed, and you’re tolerating food well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your tacrolimus from 1 mg to 2 mg twice a day. Sirolimus stays at 2 mg daily. This helps protect your transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why the increase?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your level was on the lower end. With diarrhea, absorption can be unpredictable. The higher dose ensures you stay protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And the loperamide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take 2 mg up to four times a day as needed. But don’t overuse it—only for loose stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Should I restart Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to 40 mg daily. But drink plenty of fluids and watch for dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your transplant team in a week for lab work. And we’ve scheduled a GI appointment to look into the recurring diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling really good. Any last instructions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking all your meds as prescribed. Watch for fever, worsening diarrhea, or swelling. Call if you have chest pain or trouble breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the multivitamin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, one daily. Helps with overall nutrition, especially after fluid loss.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had a lot of health issues over the years. It’s nice to have a team that coordinates everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Your history of transplant, heart disease, and anemia means we have to be careful with every decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I’ll make sure to keep all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Your labs are stable, and you’re walking independently. Here’s your discharge summary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. We’ll see you in follow-up soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this wasn’t another infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: So are we. Staying on top of your immunosuppressants and hydration is key to avoiding future issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful with fluids, especially when I’m not feeling well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. And don’t hesitate to call your doctor at the first sign of trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve learned that the hard way. Thanks for the reminder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. But you’re doing well now. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.
